Eric,
This is not my area of expertise, but your thread made me curious
enough to try out a simple factor model with categorical indicators.
One thing that I noticed is that although we write the theoretical
model in terms of a latent continuous indicator connected to the
manifest indicator by a set of thresholds, the formal model used by
Lavaan does not appear to include any formal representation of this
continuous indicator variable or its variance.

Partable <- parTable(fit)
lavMatrixRepresentation(Partable[,1:6])

When I ran my model with std.lv <http://std.lv> as TRUE and then as FALSE the
difference had no effect on the unit variances of the indicator
variables reported in the covariance matrix.

inspect(fit, 'cov.all')

So, my hypothesis is the following:
(a) std.lv <http://std.lv> refers only to latent variables explicitly represented in
the model.
(b) the latent continuous indicators are not explicitly represented in
the model.
and thus,
(c) std.lv <http://std.lv> does not affect the scaling of the latent continuous
indicator variables to have unit variance.

Keith

Perhaps I should give some more information:

by default, if a scaled test statistic has been used (for both models),
the anova() function uses the (original) formulas from Satorra (2000)
(references below) to compute a correct 'scaled' test statistic (a
scaled chi-square difference test). Not easy to compute (and it may
fail), but you always get a positive test statistic.

You can also use the (currently undocumented) option SB.classic=TRUE, as in

anova(fit1, fit2, SB.classic=TRUE)

which will use the well-known approximate formulas from Satorra &
Bentler (2001). which are easy to compute (even by hand), but may lead
to a negative test statistic now and then. These are the formulas from
the Mplus website.

In dev 0.5-16, there is a new function 'lavTestLRT()' which has all this
properly documented.

References:

      Satorra, A. (2000). Scaled and adjusted restricted tests in
      multi-sample analysis of moment structures. In Heijmans, R.D.H.,
      Pollock, D.S.G. & Satorra, A. (eds.), Innovations in multivariate
      statistical analysis. A Festschrift for Heinz Neudecker
      (pp.233-247). London: Kluwer Academic Publishers.

      Satorra, A., & Bentler, P. M. (2001). A scaled difference
      chi-square test statistic for moment structure analysis.
      Psychometrika, 66(4), 507-514.

On 02/03/2014 11:30 AM, 金少博 wrote:
> Assume we have a sample of categorical data with sample size n. We will
> then have something like sqrt(n) (rhohat-rho) is asymptotically normally
> distributed as N(0,Pi), where Pi is the asymptotic covariance matrix of
> polychoric correlation matrix. When Lavaan computes Pi, does anyone know
> that  whether Lavaan uses n or n-1?

lavaan compute the asymptotic covariance matrix of (rhohat - rho), and
calls it WLS.W. (see eq 22 of Muthen 1984). The inverse of this matrix
(called WLS.V) is used in the WLS estimator.

To compute standard errors, we first use eq 24 of Muthen 1984, to get
the N times the asymptotic covariance matrix of the parameter vector
(theta); next, we divide by N-1 to get the final asymptotic covariance
matrix of the free parameters.

Yves.

Ah, you discovered the power=TRUE option. This was an attempt to mimic
the functionality of JruleMplus (see
https://github.com/daob/JruleMplus/wiki): to use both the EPC and the
power of the MI test to detect model misspecification.

I coded this a few years back, and it was not ready yet, because I could
(at the time) only provide unstandardized values for 'delta'
(representing the effect size). So consider this option as 'experimental'.

The 'flags' in the decision column are as follows:

- "***": significant MI and low power
- "epc": significant MI but also high power
- "(i)": non-significant MI and low power
- (nothing): non-significant MI and high power

in decreasing order of needing your attention...

On 02/09/2014 09:57 PM, Mijke Rhemtulla wrote:
> I just encountered this same issue. Thanks for clarifying how lavaan
> defines the baseline model. I noticed also that if I specify exogenous
> covariances in the model statement, then lavaan uses a model baseline
> that includes independence of exogenous variables (so I get more degrees
> of freedom in the baseline model). It makes some sense, but I wasn't
> expecting it. E.g., mod2 below gives me a baseline model with 10 df,
> whereas mod1 gives 9. I actually like that I can use this to decide what
> I want the baseline model to be, but is this supposed to happen?

Yes.

> mod1 <- '
> AA ~ SRL
> FG ~ AA + SGG
> SGG ~ PGG + AA #-- baseline model has 9 df
> '

Ok, here we have the 'usual' setting where we have 5 observed variables,
2 of them are exogenous. The total covariance matrix is 5*6/2=15
'datapoints', but we do not count the exogenous variances/covariances
(because they are fixed). Therefore, we only have 15 - 3 = 12
'datapoints'. In the independence model, we only estimate the variances
of the endogenous variables (3 free parameters), but the
variances/covariances of the fixed exogenous variables remain fixed at
their sample values. Hence, we have 12 - 3 = 9 degrees of freedom.

> mod2 <- '
> AA ~ SRL
> FG ~ AA + SGG
> SGG ~ PGG + AA
> SRL ~~ PGG  # explicitly specify the covariance between exogenous
> predictors -- baseline model has 10 df
> '

Here, by explicitly adding the covariance between exogenous predictors
(note that you get a warning if you do this), they are 'upgraded' to
random variables. Hence, their variances/covariances are not fixed. We
have now 15 datapoints (instead of 12), and the independence model now
estimates 5 variances (instead of 3), resulting in 15 - 5 = 10 degrees
of freedom...

BTW, lavaan dev 0.5-16 adds a 'baseline.model' argument to the
fitMeasures() function, so that users can specify their own baseline models.

Yves.

Some statements/questions on how to interpret output of lavaan for path analysis. If you disagree with any statement, please respond.

1. I see the value of "Minimum Function Test Statistic" (chisq) for my model (user model) and the baseline model (which assumes that there exists no path between any pair of variables).

The lower the "Minimum Function Test Statistic", the better is my model. Correct?

3. The closer the CLI and TLI to 0.95, the better is my model.

4. The lower the RMSEA, the better is my model. (RMSEA of .1 means that the model moderately fits the data).

I should check for the path which has the highest values of mi (mi is the change in chisq value of the model if I set free the focal path) and epc (expected change in parameter estimate if I set free the focal path). I can then modify my model such that I unrestrain the chosen path (which has the highest mi and epc). My modified model will now have one lower df than my initial model.
8. Should I look at any sepc* column in the output of modindices?

9. I should regenerate the fit summary and the mod indices. I can also compare the chisq value for the two models - the modified model should have lower chisq.

10. I cannot use AIC and BIC if I am comparing my model with the null/baseline model. I can use them only if I have two user models to compare. Right?

1.  In an abstract sense, yes.  Chi-square measures discrepancy, and less is better.
2.  No.  H0 is that your model is correct in the population, and all supporting assumptions also hold.  A low p-value means that this compound hypothesis is unlikely to be true, given the data.
3.  No.  The maximum value for CFI is 1.0  CFI achieves this value whenever your chi-square is equal to or less than degrees of freedom.  TLI is not normed in this way, so its value can exceed 1.0 in some situations.
4.  Yes / no.  Arbitrary rules of thumb vary, but RMSEA = 0.1 or larger is a poor fit.  Some say that RMSEA less than equal to .05 or .06 is a good approximate fit, but passing this "test" is not the same as passing the chi-square test.
5.  H0 for the "test of close fit" is RMSEA less than or equal to .05.
6.  SRMR is a measure of discrepancy not tied to chi-square.  Some say that SRMR less than or equal to .05 indicates a good approximate fit.
7.  You are formally correct about the DF loss, though that is hardly an adequate penalty for capitalization on chance, since you have, effectively, peeked at ALL of the modification index values.
8.  I think standardized parameter estimates are dumb, but that's just me (and all right-thinking statisticians--but I digress).
9.  The modified model must have a lower chi-square.  The decrease must be at least as large as the modification index, but can be much larger.
10.  AIC and BIC serve their model comparison function even is one of the models is the null model.  If your target model does not look better than the null model--using any criterion--then your model is not well-supported by the data.

Hi everyone,

I'm currently in the process of implementing Satorra and Bentler (2010)'s revised scaled chi-square difference test (cited at the end of this post) in R using lavaan, however I've run into a bit of a snag. However, this run never converges, and thus, the chi-square value is not obtainable. I've been trying to find a work-around using the control= parameter, but have not had much luck. I do not have a strong understanding of what is actually going on under the hood of the control= parameter, and have mostly just been adjusting values haphazardly, hoping for a useful outcome.

On 02/19/2014 01:27 AM, Randy B wrote:

> verb1 ~~ rv1*verb1
> verb2 ~~ rv1*verb2
> verb4 ~~ rv1*verb4
> verb6 ~~ rv1*verb6

This is dangerous syntax is a multiple group analysis (and perhaps I
should make it illegal, throwing an error).

Currently (0.5-15), this syntax will fix the (residual) variances to be
equal in the first group only. If you want them to be equal in the other
groups, you need to write something like (assuming 3 groups):

verb1 ~~ c(rv1, rv2, rv3)*verb1
verb2 ~~ c(rv1, rv2, rv3)*verb2
verb4 ~~ c(rv1, rv2, rv3)*verb4
verb6 ~~ c(rv1, rv2, rv3)*verb6

I would suggest NOT to use the group.equal="residuals" option in this
setting. If you need them to be equal both within and across groups,
just write

verb1 ~~ c(rv1, rv1, rv1)*verb1
verb2 ~~ c(rv1, rv1, rv1)*verb2
verb4 ~~ c(rv1, rv1, rv1)*verb4
verb6 ~~ c(rv1, rv1, rv1)*verb6

and all will be fine.

Yves.

messages.subject_clean: survey.lavaan giving unexpected results with missing data
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I'm using survey.lavaan to correct for clustering in a dataset, and getting unexpected results. Specifically, when I use survey.lavaan, the chi-square is inflated dramatically. I wondered if this was because of missing data.

Reproducible example below.

Summary:
I generate data with 6 items and 1000 cases to fit a single factor model.
Fitting with ML gives me chi-square of 8.5 (df = 9).

Then I randomly set ~20% of each variable to missing, and fit the model again.
Fitting with ML gives me chi-square of 10.4 (df = 9).

Then I randomly assign each case to 1 of 100 clusters (each of size 10), set up a survey design, and run survey.lavaan. Chi-square now = 24.5 (9 df).

My hunch is that the survey.lavaan is not taking into account that there is missing data. Or that I've made a mistake in my survey setup. If anyone can shed light on this, I'd be grateful.

Thanks,

Jeremy

Here is the code for the example:

set.seed(1234)

#Generate data to fit a one factor model
F <- rnorm(1000)
x1 <- rnorm(1000) + F
x2 <- rnorm(1000) + F
x3 <- rnorm(1000) + F
x4 <- rnorm(1000) + F
x5 <- rnorm(1000) + F
x6 <- rnorm(1000) + F

d <- as.data.frame(cbind(x1, x2, x3, x4, x5, x6))

d$cluster <- rep(c(1:10), 100)

cfaModel <- "f =~  x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + x5 + x6"

cfaFit <- cfa(cfaModel, data=d, estimator="ML", missing="ml", std.lv <http://std.lv>=FALSE)
summary(cfaFit)

#Randomly set ~20% of cases to missing
dm <- d

dm$x1 <- ifelse(runif(1000) < 0.2, NA, d$x1)
dm$x2 <- ifelse(runif(1000) < 0.2, NA, d$x2)
dm$x3 <- ifelse(runif(1000) < 0.2, NA, d$x3)
dm$x4 <- ifelse(runif(1000) < 0.2, NA, d$x4)
dm$x5 <- ifelse(runif(1000) < 0.2, NA, d$x5)
dm$x6 <- ifelse(runif(1000) < 0.2, NA, d$x6)

#Fit missing data model
cfaFitm <- cfa(cfaModel, data=dm, estimator="ML", missing="direct", std.lv <http://std.lv>=FALSE)
summary(cfaFitm)

#Set up survey design
survey.design <- svydesign(ids=~cluster, probs=NULL, data=dm)

#Correct for clustering
cfaFitms <- lavaan.survey(cfaFitm, survey.design, estimator="ML")
summary(cfaFitms)

        # If the missing argument is not specified and data have NAs, the default is fiml.

The fact that the missing argument was missing in the call to cfa() meant that the value returned by lav_samplestats_from_data() was empty, since there were no complete observations in Ya's planned missing design.

Hi Jeremy

There is a combination of issues here. One is that

    lavaan.survey(cfaFitm, survey.design, estimator="ML")

should throw an error. The fact that output is given instead of an error is a bug, which I will correct in the upcoming version. Thanks for bringing my attention to it. (An incorrect chi-square is indeed given, but this has nothing to do with the clustering. It is because the FIML-estimated variance-covariance matrix is taken as being based on 1000 cases when in fact it is much more uncertain than that due to the missing data).

Instead it should be

        lavaan.survey(cfaFitm, survey.design)

However, when you use  this with cfaFitm, an error is also thrown (correctly). The reason for that is that there is currently no implementation of the combination of FIML and survey weights/clustering/stratification. This would require an adjusted ("MLR-complex") estimator that is not implemented (yet?) in lavaan.

However, it is possible to deal with missing data by using multiple imputation. This is described in the lavaan.survey paper (accepted to the Journal of Statistical Software, preprint here: http://daob.nl/publications/ .

For your example, you could use
>
> # Fit using listwise deletion to get a starting model

You can fit the 'strong invariance' model on itself (using cfa/sem,
instead of the measurementInvariance function), and then you have access
to all the arguments of the optimizer via the control() argument (see
?nlminb for an overview).

criteria, for example:

fit <- cfa(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939,
control=list(rel.tol=1e-4))

fails, and you believe it should converge, please send me your full R
script + a snippet of the data.

messages.body_plain:
Closer to (a) though it is not that bad.

All of these statistics are approximations: SB matches the mean of the distribution, while other statistics also match the variance. The issue of difference testing is then also different for these two types of statistics. You need these in the situation of complex sampling using pseudo-ML but also (more famously) when there is nonnormality and you fit using ML (in fact this is also pseudo-ML). There are very few simulations, however, specifically using complex survey data rather than nonnormality (some were done by Asparouhov & Muthén).

What I think nobody has done yet is 1) describe exactly how you would deal with sample weights when calculating some of these variance adjusted difference tests, though this should not be too difficult to work out;  and 2) simulated chi-square _difference testing_  under complex sampling to evaluate the different approaches.

On the other hand, quite a bit of work has been done on this issue in the context of nonnormality, from which we know that SB difference testing often works well. That is why I say it is not as bad as knowing nothing.

Vivek--
     essentially, yes, that is correct.
--Ed Rigdon

Sent from my iPad

On Feb 22, 2014, at 6:19 PM, Vivek Astvansh <vivek.a...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Thank you again, Edward.
>
> So, I should read the output as follows - please tell me if I am either incomplete or incorrect or both :-)
>
> Section A: this section reports the estimator, and three pieces of info for my model: minimum function test statistic (which is the value of the discrepancy function for my model, and since this function has Chi-square distribution, this statistic is the Chi-square statistic for my model), df, and the p-value (of the earlier reported Chi-square value). The Chi-square and p-value relate to the H0 that my model is correct in the population (and that all related assumptions hold true). If p < 0.05, I should reject H0 => my model is not correct in the population.
>
> Section B: this section reports the same three pieces of info for the baseline model (which states that there is no path among any pair of variables): minimum function test statistic (again, Chi-square value for the baseline model), df, and p-value of the Chi-square statistic.
>
> Section C: this section combines the info reported in sections A and B to compare the user model against the baseline model. This comparison is done through two indices: CFI and TLI.
>
>
>
>
> On Tue, Feb 18, 2014 at 1:48 PM, Edward Rigdon <edward...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > 1.  Yes, that is so.  In much of psychological statistics, H0 is an hypothesis of "no effect," which researchers attempt to refute through gathering more evidence.  But in conventional factor-based SEM, H0 is the hypothesis that you wish to defend, and a low p-value is evidence against your model.  Paul Meehl wrote a paper in the late 60s in which he chastised psychological statistics, because rejecting the null was just a matter of getting your sample size high enough.  He might have favored the factor-based SEM arrangement, only that one gives researchers an incentive to avoid rejection by avoiding evidence, and that isn't good for science.
> > 2.  You understand MI and EPC quite well.  The hard part is, given that you have this knowledge, how do you best use it in the interests of science.  Even Joreskog and Sorbom, who pioneered MI, have had doubts about whether this was a good idea or a bad one.
> > 3.  I can't help you that one.  The answer is a matter of philosophy as much as (or more than) statistics.
> >
> >
> > On Tue, Feb 18, 2014 at 1:15 PM, Vivek Astvansh <vivek.a...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > Thank you very much, Edward. A few follow-up questions:
> > >
> > > 1. If H0 is that my model fits the data in the population, and p-value < 0.05, I should reject H0, and that is a bad news for me. This is counter-intuitive to how social scientists see H0. Social scientists see H0 as maintaining the status quo - that is, there is no effect of the intervention. Hence, rejecting H0 means a good news; means that the effect exists. Am I missing something here?
> > >
> > > 2. My second question relates to the output of modindices() function in lavaan package. As I understand, mi for a path (be it ~~ or ~) gives me the amount by which the model chisq will change after/if I were to free that path - that is, estimate the path coeff of that path, rather than constrain it to 0. Further, epc (or sepc_all) indicates how much the coeff will change after I free the path.
> > >
> > > I should look at those rows in the output of modindices() which have the highest value of sepc_all and mi, include that path in the modified model, and then reestimate.
> > >
> > > Am I complete and correct here?
> > >
> > > 3. I have seen info on how to interpret the "decision" column of the output of modindices(), but I have not understood that info. The decision column has three values: epc, ***, and i.
> > > What do they mean? Should I first focus on ***?
> > >
> > > Thank you.
> > >
> > >
> > > On Sun, Feb 16, 2014 at 10:00 PM, Edward Rigdon <edward...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > 1.  In an abstract sense, yes.  Chi-square measures discrepancy, and less is better.
> > > > 2.  No.  H0 is that your model is correct in the population, and all supporting assumptions also hold.  A low p-value means that this compound hypothesis is unlikely to be true, given the data.
> > > > 3.  No.  The maximum value for CFI is 1.0  CFI achieves this value whenever your chi-square is equal to or less than degrees of freedom.  TLI is not normed in this way, so its value can exceed 1.0 in some situations.
> > > > 4.  Yes / no.  Arbitrary rules of thumb vary, but RMSEA = 0.1 or larger is a poor fit.  Some say that RMSEA less than equal to .05 or .06 is a good approximate fit, but passing this "test" is not the same as passing the chi-square test.
> > > > 5.  H0 for the "test of close fit" is RMSEA less than or equal to .05.
> > > > 6.  SRMR is a measure of discrepancy not tied to chi-square.  Some say that SRMR less than or equal to .05 indicates a good approximate fit.
> > > > 7.  You are formally correct about the DF loss, though that is hardly an adequate penalty for capitalization on chance, since you have, effectively, peeked at ALL of the modification index values.
> > > > 8.  I think standardized parameter estimates are dumb, but that's just me (and all right-thinking statisticians--but I digress).
> > > > 9.  The modified model must have a lower chi-square.  The decrease must be at least as large as the modification index, but can be much larger.
> > > > 10.  AIC and BIC serve their model comparison function even is one of the models is the null model.  If your target model does not look better than the null model--using any criterion--then your model is not well-supported by the data.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > On Sun, Feb 16, 2014 at 10:26 PM, Vivek Astvansh <vivek.a...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > >
> > > > > Some statements/questions on how to interpret output of lavaan for path analysis. If you disagree with any statement, please respond.
> > > > >
> > > > > 1. I see the value of "Minimum Function Test Statistic" (chisq) for my model (user model) and the baseline model (which assumes that there exists no path between any pair of variables).
> > > > >
> > > > > The lower the "Minimum Function Test Statistic", the better is my model. Correct?
> > > > >
> > > > > 2. The H0 in this chisq test is that my model does not fit the data any better than the baseline model. If the p-value of the chisq value of my model is < 0.05, I should infer that my model fits the data better than the baseline model.
> > > > >
> > > > > 3. The closer the CLI and TLI to 0.95, the better is my model.
> > > > >
> > > > > 4. The lower the RMSEA, the better is my model. (RMSEA of .1 means that the model moderately fits the data).
> > > > >
> > > > > 5. My RMSEA is .1, but the p-value of RMSEA <= 0.05 is 0.000. How can this be?
> > > > > 6. How can I infer SRMR?
> > > > >
> > > > > 7. I next retrieve modIndices for each possible path in the model. I should check for the path which has the highest values of mi (mi is the change in chisq value of the model if I set free the focal path) and epc (expected change in parameter estimate if I set free the focal path). I can then modify my model such that I unrestrain the chosen path (which has the highest mi and epc). My modified model will now have one lower df than my initial model.
> > > > > 8. Should I look at any sepc* column in the output of modindices?
> > > > >
> > > > > 9. I should regenerate the fit summary and the mod indices. I can also compare the chisq value for the two models - the modified model should have lower chisq.
> > > > >
> > > > > 10. I cannot use AIC and BIC if I am comparing my model with the null/baseline model. I can use them only if I have two user models to compare. Right?
> > > > >

messages.body_plain:
> *What does this error message mean? Should I be concerned about this?*

> Warning message:
> In vnames(FLAT, "ov.x", warn = TRUE) :
>    lavaan WARNING: model syntax contains variance/covariance/intercept
> formulas
>    involving (an) exogenous variable(s): [MEAN_F_Com MEAN_M_Tru
> MEAN_M_Com MEAN_F_Tru];
>    Please use fixed.x=FALSE or leave them alone

By default, lavaan treats exogenous variables as fixed. This means that
you do not need to specify their covariances. So, you can omit this part
of the model syntax:

      # correlated predictors
      MEAN_M_Tru ~~ MEAN_M_Com
      MEAN_M_Tru ~~ MEAN_F_Tru
      MEAN_M_Tru ~~ MEAN_F_Com

      MEAN_M_Com ~~ MEAN_F_Tru
      MEAN_M_Com ~~ MEAN_F_Com

      MEAN_F_Tru ~~ MEAN_F_Com

      MEAN_COM ~~ MEAN_EXP

But this will not affect the results.

> *Why does lavaan automatically correlate the residuals of my outcome
> variables?*

>    MEAN_GAD ~~
>      MEAN_SLS         -0.024    0.013   -1.810    0.070   -0.024   -0.050
>      MEAN_SCC         -0.069    0.008   -8.822    0.000   -0.069   -0.253
>    MEAN_SLS ~~
>      MEAN_SCC          0.078    0.017    4.553    0.000    0.078    0.127

Because we believe it is a sensible thing to do. Of course, if you do
not like lavaan's defaults, you should use the lavaan() function instead.

To learn how to test for indirect effects, please read section 7.4 of
the lavaan paper (see lavaan.org <http://lavaan.org> website for the link), and see the
examples here:

http://www.da.ugent.be/cvs/pages/en/Presentations/Presentation%20Yves%20Rosseel.pdf

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
thank you for that.

since you're a SEM beginner the lavaan board is probably not the best place to start asking these questions since they're not directly related to the uses and application of lavaan. perhaps you could get a lot more guidance if you posted your question on the SEMNet listserv (just google 'SEMNET' and its the first link you'll get) where SEM experts gather to discuss SEM issues and answer questions.

in any case, my (very, very quick) 2 cents:

the chi-square VS no chi-square fit is an ongoing issue. experts do not quite agree on whether the chi-square test should be an absolute deal-breaker (i.e. abandon the model if it doesn't fit) or just a pointer. the consensus however seems to be towards the fact that not fitting by the chi-square test is not too-big of a deal. the problem comes down to the null hypothesis that it tests (i.e. Ho: Model-implied-covariance = Sample covariance). notice the '=' sign there? it's not an approximate sign. it's an equal one... which formally states that you have the EXACT model of the population, and everything else is sample variability. as your sample size gets larger and larger, even the tiniest deviations (maybe small cross-loadings or minor correlated residuals, etc.) will be caught on by the test and yield a p-value < .05. this is why so many approximate fit indices exist, since they recognize the fact that, maybe, slight deviations from the true population model are not too-big-of-a-deal. so, all in all, i'd say more experts agree than not that a significant chi-square test should not deter you from continue with using your model.

but i'm pretty sure that if you post this same question on SEMNet you are going to get a few people (Les Hayduk come to mind) who would tell you that without chi-square fit your model is strongly suspect. but he's in the minority, so you should be OK ;-)
